# One fine coordinate: height-sensitive cap sampling and exact planar mass

This note proves a sharp absolute sampling estimate with **one** fine lattice coordinate and any continuous dimension s >= 1. It then gives an exact planar identity for bodies reconstructed from their sampled fibers. The relative parameter is the fine spacing divided by the projection length, or an explicitly displayed sampled-mass ratio. Small absolute coarse volume alone does not imply a heavy sampled fiber, even when the full two-level convex hull is uniformly round and is exactly the hull of its mixed set.

No depth-continuity claim from weak convergence and no general mixed-integer depth theorem is used.

## 1. Sharp absolute cap discrepancy in every continuous dimension

Let Q be any nonempty compact convex subset of R_u x R^s_x, where s >= 1. It need not have full dimension. Let

- G = t + h Z, with h > 0 and arbitrary real coset t;
- f(u) = vol_s(Q_u), where Q_u = {x : (u,x) belongs to Q};
- W = sup_u f(u);
- A = vol_(s+1)(Q), and A_h = h sum_(u in G) f(u).

Empty fibers have volume zero. All these quantities are finite. For every closed ambient halfspace H, including one whose continuous normal is zero, put

A(H) = vol_(s+1)(Q intersect H),
A_h(H) = h sum_(u in G) vol_s((Q intersect H)_u).

Then

    |A_h(H) - A(H)| <= h W.                                  (1)

The same estimate holds for the whole source and for open halfspaces. Its constant 1 is optimal.

**Proof.** Write g(u) = vol_s((Q intersect H)_u). Brunn--Minkowski in the x coordinates gives concavity of g^(1/s) on the interval where the sections are nonempty. In particular every strict positive superlevel

    I_a = {u : g(u) > a},  a > 0,

is an interval, possibly empty or a singleton. It may have either, both, or neither endpoint included. For every bounded interval I with any such endpoint convention,

    |h #(G intersect I) - length(I)| <= h.                   (2)

Indeed, if I contains k >= 1 grid points, the distance between the first and last is (k-1)h, while its length is at most (k+1)h; the endpoint conventions determine only whether either limiting equality is attainable. If k = 0, its length is at most h. Singletons satisfy the same estimate.

Since 0 <= g <= W, layer cake and Tonelli give

    A_h(H) - A(H)
      = integral_0^W [h #(G intersect I_a) - length(I_a)] da.

This proves (1). The proof for an open halfspace is identical: its sections and strict superlevels are still convex, measurable, and bounded. Neither closure nor positive (s+1)-volume was needed.

For sharpness take Q = [0,Nh] x K, t = 0, where N >= 1 and K is any compact s-dimensional convex body of volume W. Then A_h - A = h W. A vertical body Q = {t} x K also attains equality with A = 0. Thus (1) retains, rather than discards, whole positive-volume sampled fibers on a closed boundary. QED.

## 2. Relative discrepancy depends on projection length

Let the projection of Q onto R_u be [a,b], of length L = b-a > 0. If W > 0, then

    L W/(s+1) <= A <= L W.                                  (3)

**Proof.** Choose u_0 with f(u_0) arbitrarily close to W. For u between a and u_0, convexity using any point of Q_a and the full section Q_(u_0) gives

    f(u) >= f(u_0) ((u-a)/(u_0-a))^s.

The analogous right-hand bound uses b. Integrating both sides gives A >= L f(u_0)/(s+1). If u_0 is an endpoint, only the other side is needed. Let f(u_0) increase to W. The upper bound is immediate. This also proves A > 0 under the displayed hypotheses, without an initial full-dimensionality assumption. QED.

The factor s+1 in (3) is sharp: a cone with a full-volume section at one projection endpoint and a point at the other attains equality.

Consequently, uniformly over every closed halfspace,

    |A_h(H)-A(H)|/A <= eta := h W/A <= (s+1)h/L.             (4)

If eta < 1, then A_h > 0 and

    |A_h(H)/A_h - A(H)/A| <= 2 eta/(1-eta).                 (5)

For (5), subtract the ratios, use A(H) <= A, |A_h-A| <= eta A, and A_h >= (1-eta)A. This is only a convenient normalized bound; the asserted sharp constant concerns the absolute inequality (1).

Thus L/h -> infinity implies uniform relative all-cap approximation, independently of how small the continuous heights or A become. If normalized cap discrepancies stay bounded away from zero along a sequence with A > 0, then L/h must be bounded along a subsequence. Bounded L/h is a necessary condition for such failure, not a sufficient one.

For finitely many coarse levels z, apply (1) to every restricted halfspace and sum:

    |sum_z A_(h,z)(H) - sum_z A_z(H)| <= h sum_z W_z.        (6)

When every level has positive A_z and projection length L_z,

    h sum_z W_z / sum_z A_z
      <= (s+1) sum_z (A_z/sum A) h/L_z.                    (7)

A zero-(s+1)-volume level with a positive s-volume sampled vertical fiber must be retained separately; (1) still applies to it, while (4) does not.

These statements respect every block affine map

    u' = a u + c,    x' = T x + b u + d,

with a != 0 and invertible T. Specifically h' = |a|h, L' = |a|L, W' = |det T|W, and A' = |a det T|A. Both eta and h/L are unchanged. The transformed lattice is its actual coset aG+c. This is a one-fine-coordinate criterion and does not assert a common block normalization across different coarse components.

## 3. Exact trapezoid identity for grid-hull polygons

Now s = 1. Suppose additionally

    Q = conv(Q intersect (G x R)).                          (8)

Assume Q is nonempty. The grid fibers meeting Q have consecutive indices j=a,...,b. Write N=b-a+1, their lengths w_j >= 0, and T = sum_(j=a)^b w_j. Projection endpoints of Q belong to G: compactness leaves only finitely many grid fibers in (8), and the projection is their convex hull.

At an intermediate base between consecutive grid points, the actual interval fiber is exactly the Minkowski interpolation of the two adjacent sampled fibers. Here is a short proof. The sampled lower endpoints are convex and the upper endpoints concave. Their piecewise-affine interpolants are respectively convex and concave, so the region between them is convex and contains all sampled fibers. Conversely its strips are convex hulls of adjacent sampled fibers. Hence it equals Q. This is also the d=1 instance of `candidate f7422e63e37f7d98`.

The widths w_j form a nonnegative concave sequence. With

    E = (w_a+w_b)/2,

where the same endpoint is counted twice if N=1, exact integration gives

    A = h(T-E).                                            (9)

For N=1 this states A=0 and E=T, correctly retaining a possible positive vertical segment. For N>=2, the concavity chords imply

    T >= N E,
    (1-1/N) T <= A/h <= T.                                 (10)

Indeed sum the pointwise lower bound by the affine chord joining the endpoint widths. The lower inequality is sharp for affine width sequences; the upper is attained when both endpoint widths vanish. In particular every noncollapsed projection, N>=2, satisfies

    T <= 2A/h.                                             (11)

Zero-width horizontal or oblique segments are included: then T=A=0.

## 4. Two coarse levels: the exact concentration parameter

Let Q_0,Q_1 satisfy (8), with a common h and coset (different cosets would not change the argument). Their hull at coarse integer coordinates z=0,1 has exactly these endpoint slices. Put

    M = A_0+A_1,    T = T_0+T_1 > 0,
    w_* = max_(z,j) w_(z,j).

The original unweighted H_1 sampled mass is T, while the fine covolume-weighted mass is hT. Equations (9) give

    T = M/h + E_0+E_1,
    E_0+E_1 <= 2w_*.

Therefore

    w_*/T >= (1/2)(1-M/(hT))_+.                            (12)

In particular M/(hT) -> 0 implies a fiber of asymptotic mass fraction at least 1/2, hence certainly at least 1/4. Absolute M=o(h) alone gives no such conclusion because T may also tend to zero.

There is a stronger structural form. Let T_nc be the sampled mass on coarse levels with at least two nonempty grid fibers. Then

    T_nc <= 2M/h.                                          (13)

Consequently all but at most 2M/h of the sampled mass lies on coarse levels whose projection is a single grid point. With only two coarse levels, each such level is itself one fine fiber. If precisely one collapsed level has positive sampled mass, that single fiber has fraction at least

    1 - 2M/(hT).                                           (14)

This is an exact sampling/concentration dichotomy for the stated grid-hull class. It is not an allocation theorem for arbitrarily many coarse levels or varying-dimensional intrinsic limits.

## 5. Uniformly round counterexample to absolute-area concentration

Take h=1/N, epsilon=h^2, with integer N>=1. In coordinates (z,u,x), define

    Q_0 = { -1<=u<=1, |x-u|<=epsilon },
    Q_1 = { -1<=u<=1, |x+u|<=epsilon },
    C_epsilon = conv(({0} x Q_0) union ({1} x Q_1)).

Every vertex has z in {0,1} and u in hZ. Thus, for the actual fine mixed set

    S_epsilon = C_epsilon intersect (Z x hZ x R),

we have C_epsilon = conv(S_epsilon) exactly. The only coarse integer levels are 0 and 1, and every one of their 2N+1 fine fibers has length 2epsilon.

Consequently

    M = 8epsilon = 8h^2 = o(h),
    T = 4epsilon(2N+1),
    w_*/T = 1/[2(2N+1)] -> 0,
    M/(hT) = 2/(2+h) -> 1.                                (15)

So even the proposed 1/4 concentration conclusion fails under M=o(h).

This example has uniform full-hull geometry. It contains the fixed tetrahedron

    C_0 = conv{(0,1,1),(0,-1,-1),(1,1,-1),(1,-1,1)},

whose exact inequalities are

    |u+x| <= 2(1-z),     |u-x| <= 2z.

At c=(1/2,0,0), each of its four facet distances is 1/sqrt(6): the facet normals have norm sqrt(6) and slack 1. Thus the fixed block affine normalization

    F(z,u,x) = sqrt(6) (z-1/2,u,x)

gives

    unit ball subset F(C_epsilon) subset ball of radius 6. (16)

For the outer containment use epsilon<=1 and C_epsilon subset [0,1] x [-1,1] x [-2,2]; after centering and scaling its radius is at most sqrt(126)/2 < 6. F also transforms the lattice to its exact base coset, with fixed scaling sqrt(6). All ratios and the asymptotics in (15) survive, including small coarse area compared to the transformed fine spacing.

The two separate block maps

    (u,x) -> (u,(x-u)/epsilon) on Q_0,
    (u,x) -> (u,(x+u)/epsilon) on Q_1

send the components to the same square [-1,1]^2 and keep fine spacing h. In accordance with (4), both original components already have relative all-cap sampling error at most h: each has L=2 and s=1. This example therefore distinguishes small absolute coarse volume from actual relative mesh failure. It does not contradict componentwise relative sampling recovery.

## Scope

The new estimates are (1), with sharp constant 1 for one fine variable, and the exact grid-hull identity (9), with consequences (12)--(14). The uniformly round family (15)--(16) refutes concentration from absolute M=o(h). Lower-rank concentration can instead be forced by the explicitly stronger ratio M/(hT)->0. No sharp global mixed-depth budget is inferred from these identities.
